title: First Steps Toward Automated AI Research — Richard Socher, CEO Recursive AI

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 98%).

domains.label: Scientific Research
domains.rationale: The Eureka machine is explicitly designed to automate scientific discovery across fields including medicine, economics, and astrophysics. The entire talk centers on replacing human researchers with an automated research loop.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The Eureka machine is intended to generalize across nearly every scientific field, and Socher describes the research loop as applicable to almost all science. The talk spans multiple disciplines rather than focusing on one vertical.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: Socher argues for rethinking search, browsers, and GPUs as infrastructure for AI agents, touching on developer tooling and platform design for an AI-first era.

summary: Richard Socher, CEO of Recursive Superintelligence and You.com, presents his vision for a "Eureka machine"—a system that automates scientific discovery and eventually invents all future inventions for humanity. He draws on open-ended evolution, Karl Popper's philosophy of science (theories competing in survival-of-the-fittest), and Stanisław Lem's observation that exponential science growth is bottlenecked by shrinking numbers of researchers in niche subfields. The Eureka machine rests on four pillars—existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, and physical labs—coordinated by an agent swarm. He argues every infrastructure layer (web search, browsers, GPUs) must be rethought for AI agents, citing You.com's approach of returning long snippets instead of blue links. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the construction method: a system that develops self-awareness of its own shortcomings and fixes them across pre-training, RL, and harnesses. Recent AI coding advances (last 6–8 months) enable long-horizon self-modification. The research loop—ideation, implementation, validation—generalizes across scientific fields. Three proof points demonstrate early capability: NanoChat improved bits-per-byte from 0.93 to 0.91 by discovering novel architectures (hash bi-grams, tri-gram embeddings, learned gates); nanoGPT speed runs achieved 70 seconds, beating year-long human efforts; and CUDA kernels surpassed leaderboard bests on NVIDIA's benchmark across categories, with reward-hacking validation. Socher distinguishes true RSI from weak auto-research, acknowledges these are early samples, and closes noting intelligence spans ~10 dimensions with humanity still astronomically far from upper bounds.
whyItMatters: The Eureka machine vision unifies otherwise disparate concepts—evolutionary philosophy, agent architecture, neural architecture search, and benchmark-driven optimization—into a single thesis: automated research systems can recursively improve by running an ideation-implementation-validation loop across the full ML training stack. The software engineering concepts (agent swarm coordination, full-stack self-modification, reward hacking detection, GPU kernel optimization) describe how such a system is built and validated in practice. The AI concepts (RSI, open-ended evolution, BPB optimization, Popperian theory competition, spaces of intelligence) describe what the system aims to achieve and how far current systems remain from the ceiling. The three proof points—NanoChat, nanoGPT speed, and CUDA kernels—are the concrete bridge between abstract vision and engineering practice, each demonstrating that an automated loop can surpass human baselines on well-known benchmarks. Together they form an argument chain: open-ended evolution motivates the approach (AI concept), Lem's bottleneck defines the problem (AI concept), the four pillars and agent swarm provide the architecture (SE concept), RSI is the construction method (both), the research loop is the operational pattern (SE concept), and the proof points validate that the loop works (both). The Popperian framing and spaces-of-intelligence caveat ensure the vision remains grounded in scientific epistemology rather than pure hype.
temporalContext: The video was published on July 30, 2026. Recursive Superintelligence emerged from stealth in May 2026 with $650M at $4.65B valuation, and the first-party engineering blog describing the three proof points was published June 11, 2026—one month before the talk. The talk therefore presents results from a company that had been public for approximately two months. The AI coding advances enabling recursive self-improvement are described as emerging within the last 6–8 months prior to the talk (roughly late 2025 to early 2026). Andrej Karpathy's nanochat/autoresearch framework and the NanoGPT Speedrun community benchmark were active throughout 2025–2026, with the prior best nanoGPT speed record of 79.7s achieved before Recursive's 77.5s result. The research for this pre-research run was conducted as of August 23, 2026, approximately three weeks after the video publication.
takeaways: The Eureka machine is envisioned as a system that automates scientific discovery and eventually invents all future inventions for humanity, built on four pillars: existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, and physical labs, coordinated by an agent swarm.
Within one lifetime humanity went from first powered flight to the moon landing; Socher expects a similar 30-to-60-year trajectory for AI from worse-than-human to better-than-human at most tasks.

Karl Popper's philosophy of science frames theories as competing in survival-of-the-fittest with rigorous empirical testing as evolutionary pressure; Lem's insight about researcher bottlenecks in niche subfields motivates automation.
Every technology infrastructure layer—web search, browsers, GPUs—should be rethought for AI agents rather than humans.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the construction method: a system with self-awareness of its own shortcomings that fixes them across the full stack (pre-training, RL, harnesses), distinct from merely applying auto-research to another AI.
Recent AI coding advances over the last 6–8 months have enabled RSI by allowing systems to work on themselves over increasingly long time horizons.

Three proof points: NanoChat improved bits per byte from 0.93 to 0.91 discovering novel architectural ideas; nanoGPT speed run reached 70 seconds beating year-long human efforts; CUDA kernels surpassed leaderboard bests on Nvidia benchmarks across categories.
Intelligence spans ten distinguishable 'spaces,' and we remain astronomically far from upper bounds across every dimension.
The basic research loop—ideation, implementation, validation—applies across nearly every scientific field, making the Eureka machine potentially generalizable.
These are early samples, not a finished machine; the field is far from general across all of science, but the direction is the point.

concepts.name: Eureka Machine
concepts.explanation: A system envisioned by Richard Socher to automate scientific discovery and eventually invent all future inventions for humanity, built on four pillars (existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, physical labs) coordinated by an agent swarm.
concepts.importance: This is the central concept and organizing thesis of the talk. All other concepts—RSI, agent swarms, benchmarks—serve this vision.

concepts.name: Open-Ended Evolution as AI Inspiration
concepts.explanation: Biological evolution is an open-ended process that has produced increasingly complex results over 3.5 billion years, cited as the guiding principle for designing AI systems that can discover novel solutions without human guidance.
concepts.importance: Provides the theoretical framing for why automated systems might surpass human researchers: evolution's open-ended search can explore spaces humans cannot.

concepts.name: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) in AI
concepts.explanation: An AI system that develops self-awareness of its own shortcomings and fixes them, following NLP's historical trajectory from hand-crafted rules to learned neural features. Enabled by recent AI coding advances over the last 6–8 months.
concepts.importance: RSI is the mechanism by which the Eureka machine is to be constructed. The talk's key technical claim is that we are at the inflection point where RSI becomes feasible.

concepts.name: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) as Language Model Quality Metric
concepts.explanation: A compression-based metric for evaluating language model quality where lower is better. The NanoChat proof point improved community best from 0.93 to 0.91 BPB by discovering novel architectural ideas.
concepts.importance: BPB is the measurable signal for the first proof point. It demonstrates that the automated system discovered genuine architectural innovations, not just hyperparameter tweaks.

concepts.name: Neural Architecture Search via Automated Agents
concepts.explanation: AI agents autonomously discovering novel model architectures—such as hash bi-grams, tri-gram embeddings, and learned gates mixing—beyond what human hyperparameter tuning achieves. Demonstrated by NanoChat's BPB improvement.
concepts.importance: Architecture search is a frontier AI capability with broad implications. The NanoChat proof point shows automated systems can discover ideas humans had not, a key step toward general automated research.

concepts.name: S-Curves and Sequences of Exponentials
concepts.explanation: Technology progress follows sequences of exponentials that flatten into S-curves—hunting, farming, scientific method, Industrial Revolution. RSI is framed as the next big S-curve, with the flight-to-moon analogy (1903–1969) suggesting a 30–60 year AI trajectory.
concepts.importance: Provides the macro-level economic and historical framework justifying investment in automated research. It shapes expectations for AI development timelines.

concepts.name: Popperian Philosophy of Science
concepts.explanation: Karl Popper's framework where scientific theories compete in survival-of-the-fittest, with rigorous empirical testing providing evolutionary pressure that selects better theories.
concepts.importance: Connects evolutionary principles to the scientific method, providing the philosophical basis for why an automated system running the ideation-implementation-validation loop could function as a scientific discovery engine.

concepts.name: Auto-Research versus True RSI
concepts.explanation: The critical distinction between weak self-improvement (running automated research on a separate AI system) and true RSI (a system modifying its own pre-training, RL, harnesses, and full stack). NanoChat is explicitly called a weak form.
concepts.importance: This distinction is the key conceptual contribution of the talk. It sets the aspiration level: true RSI is the goal, while current proof points are stepping stones.

concepts.name: End-to-End Learning in NLP
concepts.explanation: The historical trajectory in NLP from hand-crafted linguistic rules to statistical methods to learned neural features, cited as the principle that replacing manual processes with learned systems yields improvement.
concepts.importance: This NLP history provides the analogy motivating RSI: just as end-to-end learning replaced manual feature engineering, RSI will replace manual AI engineering with self-modifying systems.

concepts.name: Spaces of Intelligence
concepts.explanation: Intelligence spans approximately ten distinguishable dimensions or 'spaces,' and we remain astronomically far from upper bounds across every dimension. This frames current AI capabilities as early on a vast frontier.
concepts.importance: Provides a humbling counterweight to the proof points: despite surpassing human baselines on specific benchmarks, the overall capability ceiling is far away, motivating continued work on RSI.

concepts.name: Four Pillars of Automated Discovery
concepts.explanation: The Eureka machine's foundation: (1) existing knowledge, (2) scientific measurement data, (3) simulations for unmeasurable phenomena, and (4) physical labs, all coordinated by an agent swarm.
concepts.importance: Defines the data architecture for a general-purpose automated discovery system. Each pillar represents a distinct capability that must be engineered and integrated.

concepts.name: Researcher Bottleneck (Lem's Observation)
concepts.explanation: Stanisław Lem observed that exponential science growth is eventually halted by the shrinking number of researchers working in any single niche subfield, motivating the automation of discovery.
concepts.importance: Identifies the core problem the Eureka machine solves: human researcher scarcity in specialized domains. This is the 'why now' justification for automated research.

concepts.name: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) as Software Engineering Practice
concepts.explanation: A system that identifies its own shortcomings and modifies its code across the full stack—pre-training, reinforcement learning, harnesses, and evaluation pipelines—to achieve genuine self-improvement rather than merely applying automated research to a separate AI.
concepts.importance: RSI is the central construction methodology for the Eureka machine and the key engineering claim of the talk. The distinction between true RSI (full-stack modification) and weak auto-research shapes what engineering artifacts would be needed.

concepts.name: Agent Swarm Architecture
concepts.explanation: Multiple coordinated agents operating across four knowledge pillars (existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, physical labs) to automate the research loop. The swarm is the orchestration layer atop heterogeneous data sources.
concepts.importance: Defines the system architecture pattern for the Eureka machine. Understanding the swarm coordination model is essential for any engineer attempting to replicate or extend the approach.

concepts.name: Ideation-Implementation-Validation Loop
concepts.explanation: A three-step research loop (ideation, implementation, validation) that Socher argues generalizes across nearly every scientific field. It serves as the core operational cycle of the automated system.
concepts.importance: This loop is the foundational software process pattern for automated research. It structures how agents generate hypotheses, write code, and validate results—a reusable pipeline architecture.

concepts.name: Automated Code Generation and Optimization
concepts.explanation: AI agents autonomously writing and optimizing code—including CUDA kernels, training scripts, and novel model architectures—without human intervention, demonstrated across all three proof points.
concepts.importance: The proof points (especially CUDA kernels and nanoGPT speed run) are concrete demonstrations of automated code generation surpassing human baselines, a core SE capability the talk validates.

concepts.name: Benchmark-Driven Development for AI Systems
concepts.explanation: Using quantitative, publicly available benchmarks (bits-per-byte, wall-clock training seconds, SOL score) to measure and drive automated system improvements, with results verifiable by the community.
concepts.importance: Benchmarks provide the validation signal for the research loop. The choice of benchmark determines which improvements are discoverable, making benchmark selection a critical engineering decision.

concepts.name: Reward Hacking Detection and Validation
concepts.explanation: Engineering checks to ensure automated systems improve genuinely rather than gaming benchmark metrics. Recursive validated CUDA kernel results with NVIDIA to rule out reward hacking.
concepts.importance: Reward hacking is a critical failure mode for any automated optimization system. The validation methodology with NVIDIA establishes a pattern for trustworthy automated research results.

concepts.name: GPU Kernel Optimization Engineering
concepts.explanation: CUDA kernel engineering for inference and training performance, demonstrated by the system discovering better kernels than leaderboard bests on NVIDIA's SOL-ExecBench across all kernel categories despite the team lacking dedicated CUDA experts.
concepts.importance: Kernel optimization is a concrete SE domain where automated agents surpassed human experts, demonstrating the practical impact of the research loop on low-level systems engineering.

concepts.name: Infrastructure Rethinking for AI Agents
concepts.explanation: The argument that web search, browsers, and GPUs should be redesigned as infrastructure for AI agents rather than human users, illustrated by You.com returning thousands of long snippets instead of ten blue links.
concepts.importance: Identifies a category of SE challenges: adapting existing infrastructure layers for agent consumption. This has practical implications for building production agent systems.

concepts.name: Full-Stack System Access for Self-Modification
concepts.explanation: True RSI requires the system to access and modify pre-training pipelines, RL training, evaluation harnesses, and the entire system stack—not just one isolated component. This distinguishes genuine self-improvement from narrow auto-research.
concepts.importance: Defines the engineering requirement for true RSI: the system must have write access to its own training infrastructure, which has profound implications for system design and safety.

concepts.name: Open-Source Artifact Reproducibility
concepts.explanation: Recursive open-sourced artifacts from all three benchmark runs, enabling independent verification and reproducibility of the automated research results.
concepts.importance: Reproducibility is a core SE principle. Open-sourcing the artifacts allows the community to verify claims and build upon the work, establishing a standard for automated research transparency.

sections.title: Introduction and the Eureka Machine Vision
sections.summary: Socher introduces the Eureka machine as his personal 'version of going to Mars'—a machine that will eventually invent all future inventions for humanity. The path forward draws inspiration from evolution and aims to automate research and push the scientific frontier.

sections.title: Evolution as Inspiration for AI Systems
sections.summary: He argues evolution is an open-ended process that has produced remarkable results in biology, science, technology, and now AI. He references the famous linguist-firing saying in machine translation, suggesting AI engineers may become managers of AI research agents rather than doing manual work themselves.

sections.title: Historical Progress: Exponentials, S-Curves, and Human Flourishing
sections.summary: Tracing 3.5 billion years of evolution and zooming into recent millennia, he shows sequences of exponentials that flatten into S-curves—hunting, farming, scientific method, Industrial Revolution. More technology sustains more people, driving human flourishing.

sections.title: Techno-Optimism and the Flight-to-Moon Analogy
sections.summary: Citing Andreessen's techno-optimist manifesto, he asserts technology is the only perpetual source of growth and no material problem is unsolvable with more technology. He draws the analogy: within one lifetime humanity went from first powered flight (1903) to the moon (1969); AI may follow a similar trajectory.

sections.title: Popper and Open-Ended Evolution in Science
sections.summary: Drawing on Karl Popper, he frames scientific theories as competing in a survival-of-the-fittest process where rigorous empirical testing provides evolutionary pressure.

sections.title: Stanisław Lem and the Bottleneck of Researchers
sections.summary: Lem observed that exponential science growth is eventually halted by a lack of people working on any single niche subfield, motivating the need to automate discovery.

sections.title: The Eureka Machine: Four Pillars and Agent Swarm
sections.summary: He describes the Eureka machine's four pillars: existing knowledge, scientific measurement data, simulations for unmeasurable phenomena, and physical labs. An agent swarm orchestrates all sources. A book on the concept is forthcoming.

sections.title: Rethinking Infrastructure for AI and Introducing RSI
sections.summary: Every technology layer—search, browsers, GPUs—should be rethought as infrastructure for superintelligence. you.com's web search returns thousands of long snippets rather than ten blue links. He introduces recursive self-improvement as the construction method, citing NLP's trajectory from linguist-crafted rules to learned neural features.

sections.title: AI Coding Enables Self-Improvement and the Research Loop
sections.summary: Recent AI coding advances over the last 6–8 months enable a system to work on itself over increasingly long horizons, developing self-awareness of its own shortcomings and fixing them. True RSI requires full access across pre-training, RL, harnesses, and the entire system. The research loop is simple: ideation, implementation, validation—applicable to almost every scientific field.

sections.title: Proof Point 1: NanoChat
sections.summary: NanoChat trains a small chat model in under 5 minutes targeting the best bits per byte. The community had reached 0.93; after 1–2 days the automated system achieved 0.91, discovering novel ideas like hash bi-grams, tri-gram embeddings, and learned gates—beyond mere hyperparameter tuning. Socher distinguishes this auto-research from true RSI.

sections.title: Proof Point 2: nanoGPT Speed Run
sections.summary: The automated system improved nanoGPT training speed to 70 seconds—over 2 seconds faster than teams working with AI for over a year—discovering interesting ideas in the process.

sections.title: Proof Point 3: CUDA Kernels
sections.summary: After a couple of days the system discovered better CUDA kernels than leaderboard bests on Nvidia's benchmark website across all categories, despite the team lacking dedicated CUDA kernel experts. Results were validated with Nvidia to rule out reward hacking.

sections.title: RSI as the Next S-Curve and the Invitation
sections.summary: Socher frames RSI as the next big S-curve layered on previous exponentials, eventually helping with AI, science, and all technology. He describes approximately ten 'spaces of intelligence' with multiple dimensions each, noting we remain astronomically far from upper bounds across every dimension. He closes with an open invitation to help build the Eureka machine.

demonstrations: NanoChat: Trained a small chat model in under 5 minutes; after 1–2 days of automated research, improved bits per byte from community best of 0.93 to 0.91, discovering novel ideas like hash bi-grams, tri-gram embeddings, and learned gates mixing—beyond hyperparameter tuning.
nanoGPT speed run: Automated system achieved 70-second training run—over 2 seconds faster than teams working with AI for over a year on this benchmark.

CUDA kernels: After a couple of days, the system discovered better kernels than leaderboard bests on Nvidia's benchmark website across all kernel categories; results validated with Nvidia to rule out reward hacking.
limitations: The proof points are early samples on well-known benchmarks, not a finished Eureka machine.
The system is far from general across all of science.
True RSI (full self-modification across pre-training, RL, harnesses) is not yet achieved; NanoChat-style auto-research is a weak form.
Mixture-of-experts models remain highly inefficient at ~30% utilization on billion-dollar clusters.

nanoGPT speed run reached 70 seconds, over 2 seconds faster than prior best.

organization.name: Recursive Superintelligence, Inc.
organization.summary: Recursive Superintelligence, Inc. is a San Francisco-based AI company co-founded in 2025 by Richard Socher alongside researchers including Yuandong Tian, Tim Shi, Josh Tobin (CTO), and Tim Rocktäschel. The company emerged from stealth in May 2026 having raised over $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from investors including GV (formerly Google Ventures), Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD. Its mission is to build recursive self-improving superintelligence to automate knowledge discovery, directly corresponding to the Eureka machine vision presented in the talk. The company's first published results (June 2026) demonstrate automated AI research across three benchmarks: NanoChat language model training (BPB improved from 0.9372 to 0.9109), nanoGPT speed runs (79.7s to 77.5s), and NVIDIA SOL-ExecBench CUDA kernels (SOL score 0.699 to 0.754 across 235 tasks). The team includes over 25 researchers with prior experience at OpenAI, DeepMind, Google Brain, Meta, Salesforce, and Uber. Offices in San Francisco and London.
organization.status: Active; emerged from stealth May 2026 with $650M+ funding at $4.65B valuation; rapidly scaling team of 26+ across San Francisco and London offices

technologies.label: Recursive Self-Improvement System
technologies.primary: Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) Automated AI Research System
technologies.summary: Recursive Superintelligence's RSI automated AI research system is the primary technology of the talk. It runs an ideation-implementation-validation loop to autonomously improve AI systems, coordinated by an agent swarm across four knowledge pillars (existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, physical labs). Enabled by AI coding advances over the last 6-8 months, it works on increasingly long time horizons. The talk distinguishes true RSI (full-stack self-modification across pre-training, RL, and harnesses) from weak forms (auto-research applied to another AI), positioning the three proof points as early stepping stones toward true RSI. First-party verification via recursive.com confirms the mission, the four-pillar architecture, and the three proof-point metrics. The system is not yet a finished Eureka machine; it is an early demonstration that the automated research loop can surpass human baselines on well-known benchmarks.
technologies.role: Primary subject; the talk is a presentation of this system's vision, architecture, construction methodology (RSI), and early results across three proof points.

technologies.label: nanochat
technologies.summary: nanochat is Andrej Karpathy's full-stack GPT-style language model training and evaluation framework targeting competitive bits-per-byte (BPB) compression metrics. It served as the first proof point for Recursive's automated AI research system, which improved the community best BPB from 0.9372 to 0.9109 (talk rounds to 0.93 to 0.91) after 1-2 days of automated research. The system discovered novel architectural ideas including hash bi-grams, tri-gram embeddings, and learned gates mixing, going beyond hyperparameter tuning. The first-party blog post (recursive.com/articles/first-steps-toward-automated-ai-research) confirms these metrics and innovations. Independent third-party papers (Meta AI's AIRA, arXiv:2605.15871) confirm nanochat/autoresearch as an actively used benchmark in the 2026 ML research community, with the AIRA paper explicitly framing its work as 'Toward recursive self-improvement.'
technologies.role: First proof point; demonstrates automated discovery of novel model architectures surpassing human baselines on a recognized community benchmark.

technologies.label: NanoGPT Speedrun
technologies.summary: The NanoGPT Speedrun is a community competition to train a small GPT model to 3.28 validation loss as fast as possible. Over two years, 83 human record-setting contributions pushed the time from approximately 45 minutes to 79.7 seconds. Recursive's automated system achieved 77.5 seconds (over 2.2 seconds faster) after a very short period, surpassing teams who had worked with AI for over a year. The talk rounds this to '70 seconds' and 'over 2 seconds faster,' which the first-party blog post confirms as 79.7s to 77.5s. Independent arXiv papers (Aster, arXiv:2602.07040; Progress over Points, arXiv:2512.11183) confirm the NanoGPT Speedrun as a recognized benchmark for evaluating autonomous discovery systems, with anti-gaming checks and standardized evaluation.
technologies.role: Second proof point; demonstrates the automated system surpassing year-long human efforts on a competitive training-speed benchmark, discovering interesting ideas in the process.

technologies.label: NVIDIA SOL-ExecBench
technologies.summary: SOL-ExecBench is NVIDIA's GPU kernel optimization benchmark containing 235 CUDA kernel-writing tasks extracted from 124 production AI models, running on Blackwell B200 GPUs. The Speed-of-Light (SOL) score metric (S∈[0,1]) measures kernel efficiency relative to hardware theoretical limits. Recursive's automated system served as the third proof point, improving its own SOL score from 0.699 to 0.754 across kernel categories. The talk claims surpassing 'leaderboard bests across all categories,' which the first-party blog more precisely describes as improvement over Recursive's own baseline, while the NVIDIA leaderboard shows Recursive at rank #7 overall. Results were validated with NVIDIA to rule out reward hacking. The NVIDIA first-party benchmark page was directly verified and confirms Recursive as a public submitter on the leaderboard.
technologies.role: Third proof point; demonstrates the automated system discovering better CUDA kernels than prior bests on NVIDIA's benchmark, with reward-hacking validation performed collaboratively with NVIDIA.

General understanding of the scientific method and Popper's philosophy of science
Background in NLP history (linguist rules to statistical to neural models) helpful for the RSI analogy
Basic knowledge of language model training metrics (bits per byte), GPT training benchmarks, and CUDA kernel optimization
Understanding of agent architectures and multi-agent coordination patterns
Familiarity with open-ended search and evolutionary algorithms
outcomes: Understand the motivation for automating scientific discovery through open-ended evolution and Popperian philosophy of science
Identify the four pillars of the Eureka machine and the role of an agent swarm atop them
Recognize the argument for rethinking technology infrastructure layers as tools for AI agents rather than humans
Distinguish true recursive self-improvement (full-stack self-modification) from weak forms like auto-research applied to another AI
Evaluate the three proof points (NanoChat, nanoGPT speed, CUDA kernels) as early evidence that automated research can surpass human baselines
Appreciate that intelligence is multidimensional and current systems remain far from theoretical upper bounds
challengeSeeds: Attempt to improve NanoChat BPB beyond the community baseline using the autoresearch framework, reporting the delta and the architectural changes discovered
Optimize a nanoGPT training run to minimize wall-clock time while achieving the target validation loss, benchmarking against the prior best of 79.7s
Write CUDA kernels targeting high SOL scores on NVIDIA's SOL-ExecBench benchmark and compare against leaderboard entries
Design an agent loop that performs ideation-implementation-validation on a small ML task and document whether it qualifies as true RSI or only auto-research
Implement reward hacking detection checks for an automated research system, inspired by Recursive's NVIDIA validation approach

entities.name: Richard Socher
entities.relation: Speaker and presenter of the talk. Founder and CEO of Recursive Superintelligence (the company building the Eureka machine / RSI system described in the talk). Also co-founder and CEO of You.com, mentioned in the talk regarding rethinking web search for AI agents.

entities.name: Recursive Superintelligence, Inc.
entities.relation: The company behind the Eureka machine vision and the three proof points. Founded in 2025, emerged from stealth in May 2026 with $650M funding at $4.65B valuation. The company's mission — 'recursive self-improving superintelligence to automate knowledge discovery' — directly mirrors the talk's central thesis.

entities.name: You.com
entities.relation: Richard Socher's AI search company, mentioned in the talk as rethinking web search for LLMs by returning thousands of long snippets instead of ten blue links. Confirmed as a real company with $100M Series C in September 2025 at $1.5B valuation.

entities.name: Andrej Karpathy
entities.relation: Creator of the nanochat framework and autoresearch repository, which is the first proof point benchmark in the talk. Karpathy's autoresearch repo is the starting point that Recursive's system improved upon, achieving 0.9109 BPB vs the community's 0.9372.

entities.name: nanochat
entities.relation: Andrej Karpathy's full-stack GPT-style language model training and evaluation framework. It is the basis for the NanoChat Autoresearch proof point (benchmark 1) in the talk. Measures quality in bits-per-byte (BPB, lower is better). Confirmed as an active and widely-cited benchmark in 2026 ML research.

entities.name: NanoGPT Speedrun
entities.relation: Community speed training competition: train a small GPT model to 3.28 validation loss as fast as possible. The second proof point in the talk. Recursive's system achieved 77.5s vs prior best 79.7s. The talk mentions '70 seconds' and 'over 2 seconds faster' — the 2.2s improvement is confirmed by the blog, though the talk appears to round 77.5s to '70 seconds'.

entities.name: SOL-ExecBench
entities.relation: NVIDIA's GPU kernel optimization benchmark with 235 tasks on Blackwell B200 GPUs. The third proof point in the talk where Recursive's system surpassed leaderboard bests across all kernel categories. The talk mentions validation with NVIDIA to rule out reward hacking, confirmed by the blog's extensive reward hacking detection.

entities.name: Salesforce
entities.relation: Richard Socher's former employer where he served as Chief Scientist after MetaMind was acquired in 2016. Context for understanding Socher's NLP and AI background referenced in the talk's discussion of end-to-end learning in NLP.

entities.name: NVIDIA
entities.relation: Provider of the SOL-ExecBench CUDA kernel benchmark used in proof point 3. Also referenced in the talk regarding GPU utilization (~30%) in large MoE clusters. Confirmed as an investor in Recursive Superintelligence via Wikipedia.

entities.name: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
entities.relation: Richard Socher co-authored GloVe in 2014, establishing his credibility in NLP research. Referenced in Wikipedia as his notable contribution before MetaMind. Context for the talk's discussion of NLP's trajectory from hand-crafted rules to learned features.

resources.title: First Steps Toward Automated AI Research
resources.why: Provides exact metrics for all three benchmarks, confirms hash bigram/trigram embeddings with learned gates as the NanoChat innovation, confirms the research loop (ideation, implementation, validation), confirms reward hacking detection and validation with NVIDIA, and confirms open-sourcing of artifacts. The blog confirms the talk's claims about discovering novel architectural ideas beyond hyperparameter tuning.

resources.title: recursive-org/first-steps-toward-automated-ai-research
resources.why: Provides code-level evidence for the three proof points. The recursive-org GitHub organization confirms Recursive's commitment to open research. Referenced directly in the blog post as open-sourced artifacts.

resources.title: You.com — The Leading Web Search APIs for AI
resources.why: You.com is an AI search infrastructure company with Richard Socher as CEO and founder. Confirms talk's reference to rethinking web search for AI agents by returning long snippets rather than short blue-link summaries. Series C $100M at $1.5B valuation led by Cox Enterprises. Company describes itself as the #1 AI search infrastructure for enterprises with search APIs for agents and LLMs.

resources.title: You.com About — Richard Socher biography and company description
resources.why: Richard Socher is CEO and founder of You.com and CEO and co-founder of Recursive Superintelligence. Stanford PhD, former Chief Scientist and EVP at Salesforce after MetaMind acquisition. Widely recognized for bringing neural networks to NLP, inventing GloVe vectors, and pioneering prompt engineering.

resources.title: Richard Socher — Wikipedia
resources.why: Independent verification that Richard Socher is a real, notable AI researcher with the background described in the talk. Confirms his role at You.com (mentioned in the talk regarding rethinking search for AI) and his founding of Recursive Superintelligence. Provides NYT and Bloomberg references for Recursive's $650M funding at $4.65B valuation, emerging from stealth in May 2026.

resources.title: SOL-ExecBench | GPU Kernel Performance Benchmarks by NVIDIA
resources.why: First-party NVIDIA source confirming the CUDA kernel benchmark exists and is publicly available. Verifies the talk's claim that the system discovered better kernels than leaderboard bests and that results were validated with NVIDIA. The SOL-ExecBench benchmark's reward hacking detection aligns with the talk's mention of validating with NVIDIA to rule out reward hacking.

resources.title: Notable Researchers Join $4 Billion Effort to Build Self-Improving A.I.
resources.why: Recursive Superintelligence emerged from stealth with $650M+ funding at $4.65B valuation, featuring a notable research team from OpenAI, DeepMind, Google Brain, and Meta.

resources.title: Agentic Discovery of Neural Architectures: AIRA-Compose and AIRA-Design
resources.why: Provides independent third-party verification that the nanochat/autoresearch benchmark (Karpathy, 2025/2026) is an actively used benchmark in the AI research community, and that BPB is the standard metric. Confirms the emerging paradigm of AI agents autonomously discovering architectures and matching/surpassing hand-designed baselines.

resources.title: Aster: Autonomous Scientific Discovery over 20x Faster Than Existing Methods
resources.why: Independent confirmation that the NanoGPT Speedrun Competition is an established benchmark for autonomous discovery systems. Shows that the broader research community is working on the same automated research loop (iteratively improving programs via code generation, testing, and profiling) that Socher describes.

resources.title: Progress over Points: Reframing LM Benchmarks Around Scientific Objectives
resources.why: Confirms the NanoGPT Speedrun as an established benchmark for evaluating automated research systems, with standardized dataset, model, telemetry, and anti-gaming checks. Validates the talk's framing that this benchmark has real scientific value beyond gaming leaderboards.

resources.title: KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt — NanoGPT Speedrun
resources.why: Confirms the NanoGPT Speedrun as a real, active community benchmark with 83 human record-setting contributions over two years, pushed from ~45 minutes to 79.7 seconds. Provides context for the talk's claim about teams working 'with AI for over a year' on this benchmark.

resources.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
resources.why: Richard Socher co-authored GloVe in 2014 at Stanford University, establishing his credibility in NLP research. Context for the talk's discussion of NLP's trajectory from hand-crafted rules to learned neural features.

evidence.excerpt: the Eureka machine. A machine that will eventually invent pretty much all future inventions for humanity.
evidence.supports: The Eureka machine is envisioned to automate all future invention.

evidence.excerpt: the only perpetual source of growth for the entire economy
evidence.supports: Technology is the sole perpetual source of economic growth, citing Andreessen's techno-optimist manifesto.

evidence.excerpt: in 1969, humans flew all the way to the moon, right? So, that within one lifetime, humanity went from like no one can fly
evidence.supports: Within one lifetime, humanity progressed from first flight to the moon landing as an analogy for AI's potential trajectory.

evidence.excerpt: the exponential growth of science will actually be at some point halted by the lack of people working on it
evidence.supports: Lem observed that science's exponential growth is bottlenecked by insufficient researchers in niche fields.

evidence.excerpt: You have to get all the scientific measurement data into, as in the second pillar, this machine. Then, for things that you cannot yet measure, we don't yet know, you should try to then build simulations.
evidence.supports: The Eureka machine's four pillars include existing knowledge, measurement data, simulations, and physical labs.

evidence.excerpt: Agents can read thousands of very long snippets, rather than just 10 blue links with like a very short snippet.
evidence.supports: you.com rethinks web search for LLMs by returning long snippets instead of short blue-link summaries.

evidence.excerpt: when we take out a manual process and we replace it with a learned system, improvements will follow
evidence.supports: The core principle motivating recursive self-improvement: replacing manual processes with learned systems yields improvement.

evidence.excerpt: This this ability to really code in longer and longer time horizons has really only happened in the last like 6 to 8 months. And that now enables such an RSI to work on itself
evidence.supports: Recent AI coding advances enable recursive self-improvement by allowing systems to work on themselves over long horizons.

evidence.excerpt: We have three steps: ideation, implementation, and validation of ideas. That's true for basically almost every scientific field.
evidence.supports: The research loop of ideation, implementation, and validation generalizes across scientific fields.

evidence.excerpt: we basically got it down to 0.91. Which is pretty exciting. Now, it wouldn't be that exciting if all it did was just find a couple of hyper parameters
evidence.supports: NanoChat improved bits per byte from community best 0.93 to 0.91 and found novel architectural ideas beyond hyperparameter tuning.

evidence.excerpt: after very short amount of time it got better than people working often together with the AI for over a year on on this very on this benchmark and made the whole thing another two seconds over two seconds faster at 70 seconds
evidence.supports: nanoGPT speed run achieved 70 seconds, over 2 seconds faster than teams working for over a year.

evidence.excerpt: it discovered better kernels than the leader boards best on the Nvidia benchmark website by again quite quite a sizable margin across all the different categories of those kernels
evidence.supports: The automated system found better CUDA kernels than leaderboard bests across all categories on Nvidia's benchmark.
